title: The Mohs Hardness Scale Explained for Crystal Lovers
description: Understand the Mohs hardness scale from talc to diamond, see where popular crystals rank, and learn how to store a mixed collection without scratches.
html:
If you collect crystals for long enough, you will watch a favourite stone lose its polish in a pocket, or find a delicate cluster scratched by something harder in the same drawer. The Mohs hardness scale explains why. It is the quickest way to judge how a stone will behave in daily life: how it should be worn, cleansed, stored and cleaned. This guide explains the scale, gives the ten reference minerals, lists where common crystals fall, and ends with practical advice for storing a collection.

What the Mohs scale measures

In 1812 the German mineralogist Friedrich Mohs proposed ranking minerals by their ability to scratch one another. A mineral that can scratch another is harder than the one it scratches. He chose ten familiar reference minerals and numbered them from 1 to 10. Every other mineral is placed by finding which reference stone it can scratch and which scratches it.

Two things are worth remembering. First, the scale measures scratch resistance only, not toughness or stability. A diamond is the hardest natural material but can still chip along a cleavage plane. Second, the scale is ordinal, not even. The gap between 9 (corundum) and 10 (diamond) is far larger than the gap between 1 and 2.

The ten reference minerals

MohsReference mineralEveryday comparison
1TalcScratched by a fingernail, feels soapy
2GypsumScratched by a fingernail (the family of selenite)
3CalciteScratched by a copper coin
4FluoriteScratched easily by a steel knife
5ApatiteScratched by a knife with effort
6Orthoclase feldsparScratches glass poorly; scratched by a steel file
7QuartzScratches glass and steel
8TopazScratches quartz
9CorundumRuby and sapphire; scratches topaz
10DiamondScratches everything else

Useful field tools are a fingernail (about 2.5), a copper coin (about 3.5), a steel knife blade (about 5.5) and a glass plate (about 5.5). Scratch tests should be done in a hidden spot of a spare stone, and never on a polished gem you plan to keep.

Where popular crystals fall

Soft stones (below 4)

  • Selenite: 2
  • Halite: 2.5
  • Calcite: 3
  • Malachite: 3.5 to 4
  • Azurite: 3.5 to 4
  • Amber: 2 to 2.5
  • Pearl: 2.5 to 4.5

Medium stones (4 to 6)

  • Fluorite: 4
  • Lapis Lazuli: 5 to 5.5
  • Apatite: 5
  • Turquoise: 5 to 6
  • Moldavite: 5.5
  • Opal: 5.5 to 6.5
  • Obsidian: 5 to 5.5
  • Hematite: 5.5 to 6.5

Hard stones (6 to 7)

  • Moonstone: 6 to 6.5
  • Labradorite: 6 to 6.5
  • Pyrite: 6 to 6.5
  • Peridot: 6.5 to 7
  • Jade: 6 to 7

Very hard stones (7 and above)

  • Clear Quartz, Amethyst, Citrine, Rose Quartz and Agate: about 7
  • Garnet: 6.5 to 7.5
  • Emerald and Aquamarine: 7.5 to 8
  • Topaz: 8
  • Ruby and Sapphire: 9
  • Diamond: 10

Why hardness matters for everyday use

Jewelry

Household dust contains tiny particles of quartz, which sits at 7. Anything softer than 7 will slowly pick up scratches when worn daily. This is why rings of opal, pearl and turquoise need extra care, and why experienced jewelers recommend hard stones for rings and softer ones for pendants and earrings, which take less abuse.

Cleansing

Soft stones should not be rubbed with abrasive materials, scrubbed or tumbled with harder stones. Many are also water- or sun-sensitive. See our cleansing guide and water safety guide.

Handling

A tumbled stone that rides in a pocket with keys and coins (steel at about 5.5, copper at about 3.5) will pick up scars unless it is at least a 6. Save soft stones for the desk or altar.

Testing a stone at home

If you are unsure how hard a piece is, try a gentle comparison on an inconspicuous spot. Draw the corner of the stone across a spare piece of glass, a steel knife blade or a copper coin, and see which one marks the other. A stone that scratches glass is at least a 6 or 7. One that a coin scratches is below 4. Always test on an unpolished back or a spare specimen, because a scratch is permanent, and remember that this is a rough guide, not a laboratory result.

Hardness is not toughness

Mohs tells you about scratching, not breaking. Several hard stones are fragile in other ways:

  • Cleavage: topaz, kunzite and fluorite split cleanly along internal planes if struck.
  • Brittleness: obsidian and moldavite are glass, so they chip and shatter.
  • Heat sensitivity: many gems crack with a sudden temperature change.

Jade is the opposite case: it is only moderately hard, but its interlocking fibre structure makes it exceptionally tough, which is why it has been carved for thousands of years.

How to store a collection

Good storage prevents more damage than any cleansing technique. Follow these principles:

  1. Separate by hardness. Keep soft stones (below 5) in their own compartments away from quartz and harder gems. A hard stone will scratch a soft one in a shared box.
  2. Wrap or pad. Use soft cloth, tissue, small fabric pouches or foam-lined trays.
  3. Use compartments. A tackle box or jewelry organizer with dividers works well for tumbled stones and small raw pieces.
  4. Protect points. Crystal points and clusters need individual space. Never stack them.
  5. Keep out of strong light. Amethyst, rose quartz, fluorite and celestite can fade, so display them away from windows.
  6. Control humidity. Keep selenite, halite, desert rose and similar water-sensitive stones in a dry place, away from bathrooms. A few silica gel packets help.
  7. Isolate toxic or dusty stones. Label malachite, azurite and other copper minerals and keep them away from children and pets.
  8. Label what you have. A small tag with the name, origin and any known treatment saves guessing later.

A quick storage plan

If your collection is mixed, divide it into three trays: a soft tray for stones under 5, a middle tray for 5 to 7, and a hard tray for 7 and above. Add a fourth dry box for water-sensitive stones. This simple system protects almost everything you own.

Storage and handling advice is practical guidance for collectors, and crystals complement but never replace professional medical care.
